words.etymology:
From Proto-Albanian *a-tā(s), compound of proclitic particle a and demonstrative tās, from Proto-Indo-European *téh₂es, feminine plural of *tód (“that (one)”) (compare Latin istud, English that).
The accusative is from Proto-Albanian *a-tā(s), from earlier *a-tā(n)s, from *téh₂ns, and older and dialectal varieties retain ablative asosh, acosh, from a + Proto-Albanian *tsjāsu, from *ḱjéh₂su, locative of Proto-Indo-European *ḱís (“this (one)”) (compare English he).

words.etymology:
Uncertain. Multiple etymologies have been given:
*From a Proto-Albanian *w(i)tspáti, from Proto-Indo-European *wiḱpótis (“clan leader”), comparing Lithuanian viẽšpats, Avestan 𐬬𐬍𐬯𐬞𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (vīspaⁱti)), compound of *weyḱ- (“clan, extended family”) and *pótis (“master”).
*From an old compound for "Sky father": Proto-Albanian *dźie̅u ̊ + *a(t)t-, from *dyew- (“sky”) + *átta (“father”), compare Sanskrit द्यौष्पितृ (dyáuṣ-pitṛ́), Proto-Italic *djous patēr (whence Latin Iuppiter), Ancient Greek Ζεῦ πάτερ (Zeû páter). The radical zot contains the zero-grade radical of Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws. However, problems exist with the reconstructions as an unexpected -i- emerges in PA *dźie̅u ̊, and a long -ē- instead of an expected -a-. It would be better to reconstruct a PA *dᶻáu̯(h), from PPA *di̯áu̯h (*dyáwh). Also conflicting is a semantic change from "Sky Father" or "God Father" to "lord", going from the name of a chief god to the title of common men. Usually this is seen in the reverse, with God being given the title of lord. If this etymology were true, it would make Albanian unique in this.
*Most probably from Proto-Albanian *dᶻāti- < *di̯apti- < *dəi̯ápəti- < *dei̯i̯ā́(h) páti(h) < Proto-Indo-European *desi̯áh₂s pótis (“Master of the servants”). Related to Armenian տեր (ter, “owner”).

words.etymology: From Proto-Albanian *mar(en)-, from Proto-Indo-European *merh₂- (“to pack (up)”) or Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (“to assign, allot”), cognate with Ancient Greek μείρομαι (meíromai, “receive as one's portion”), Latin mereō, merx and Hittite 𒈥𒀝 (mark, “to divide a sacrifice”). Alternatively derived from Proto-Albanian *marna, a deverbative from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ (“hand”), and compared with Ancient Greek μᾰ́ρη (mắrē, “hand”), Latin manus (“hand”).

words.etymology:
Cognate to Albanian marrë; both from Proto-Albanian *marsa (from Proto-Indo-European *mergʷ- (“to flicker; to darken; to be dark”); Proto-Indo-European *h₂mergʷ- (“dark”)).
Cognate to Proto-Slavic *morkъ (“darkness”), *morxъ (“dusk, fog”), Proto-Slavic *mergъ (“brown”), Proto-Germanic *merkuz (“dark”), Ancient Greek ἀμορβός (amorbós, “dark”), Lithuanian márgas (“colorful”).
Also related to Albanian murg (“dark”), murgët (also derived from Proto-Indo-European *mergʷ- (“to flicker; to darken; to be dark”)).
